events.title: World model companies are keeping a lot of secrets
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt This week, I moderated a panel on world models at the All In conference (no relation to the podcast), and it gave me a chance to dig into one of the most mysterious corners of the AI world. The big players in the space are Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs and Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs — and while both have accumulated a lot of buzz and funding, they also rank pretty low on the trying-to-make-money scale . At their core, world models are about automating spatial intelligence , so the field could head in lots of exciting and lucrative directions, from robotics to interactive video to more complex self-driving systems. But when I started to press on where we would actually see the tech commercialized, things got foggy. The closest thing I found to an authority was Michael Rabbat, a co-founder of AMI Labs and the company’s VP of World Models, who joined me on the panel. But when I pressed him on exactly what the company was working on, he was cagey. “We’ll talk about it when we’re ready to talk about it.” Over email, he clarified, “We’re still in a research and building phase, so we’re not talking publicly about any product plans or timeline.” To be fair, AMI is less than a year old, so it’s fair enough to keep quiet. But this sort of caginess extends to the whole world-modeling space. World Labs’ Marble is probably the most fully developed product in the space, and its demos range from straightforward media creation, building explorable environments for video games, or CGI effects. There are robotics use cases too, but the whole platform seems more designed to demonstrate capabilities. That secrecy even extends to these companies’ suppliers. On the sidelines of the same conference, I spoke to Alex de Vigan, CEO of Physicl — a data supplier for the burgeoning world model business. He says he knows Physicl’s data has been useful for whatever they’re building, but he’s still in the dark about what exactly that is. “I wish they would tell us more. We could build more useful data if we knew what they were working on,” de Vigan told me. Part of the mystery comes from how versatile world models are as an idea. The simplest version is a navigable map of the world, similar to the AI models that power self-driving cars. But the same modeling approach that helps a Waymo weave through traffic could also help a humanoid robot carry boxes, or turn a few minutes of video footage into an explorable environment. AMI has already dipped its toe in manufacturing, biomedicine, robotics, and even AI software for doctors through its Nabia partnership. Surely it won’t pursue all of those — but maybe one or two of them are standing out? No one doubts that there are lots of viable businesses to be built on world model tech — and as long as it’s easy to fundraise, there’s no particular pressure to focus on one. In fact, there’s good reason not to. If AMI announced tomorrow that they had built a humanoid OpenClaw or a next-generation Hollywood rendering system, a lot of other labs would suddenly be very interested in the space. Soon, the lab would face potential competition from the other world model companies, the neolabs, and even OpenAI and Anthropic. In some ways, it’s the flip side of all that easy fundraising. Your competitors can fundraise, too — and the same money that lets you build under the radar is also funding lots of potential rivals once the path to market becomes clear. But even if that competition is inevitable, it’s best if you delay it for as long as possible, which means keeping quiet about exactly what you’re building. Cixin Liu fans will recognize this as a dark forest scenario : If you don’t know who else is in the woods, it’s best not to attract attention. This post was first published on September 18, 2026. events.title: Concerns raised over Qld's call-in process for assessing renewable projects
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Renewable energy advocates say Qld's call-in process creates uncertainty for investors, communities The Queensland government is assessing several wind turbine proposals. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) Renewable energy advocates are calling for a better framework for development processes to ensure investors are not scared off. The Queensland government is using extraordinary powers to call in energy projects, leaving both communities and investors uncertain about the future. The Queensland government says its committed to energy projects, and has more under construction or financially promised than anywhere else in the country. Renewable energy advocates say increased government intervention in wind farms projects could threaten private sector investment as Queensland works out how to best support the growth of data centres in Australia. The Queensland government is in the process of using special "call-in" powers to assess at least three renewable energy projects across the state, after cancelling the Moonlight Range Wind Farm in Central Queensland in May 2025. The call-in powers are used during exceptional circumstances where Deputy Premier and Planning Minister Jarrod Bleije believes the project needs further assessment to ensure it meets economic and environmental state interests. The projects being assessed are the Bouldercombe Battery Energy Storage System near Rockhampton and two proposed projects on the Western Downs: the Marmadua Energy Park and the Middle Creek Energy Hub. The Western Downs projects are in the same region as the proposed $32 billion data centre, the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about four hours' drive west of Brisbane. The concept model of a large-scale data centre project that has been proposed for the Western Downs. ( Supplied: Urbis ) Local federal member and Nationals MP David Littleproud has also called on the Queensland government to intervene in the federally approved $1.5 billion Tarong West Wind Farm proposed further north in the South Burnett region. This has raised concern in the Renewable Energy Alliance. National director Andrew Bray said the state government's enthusiasm for the exceptional powers could be a roadblock for investment in energy projects. Mr Bray, whose organisation advocates for the use of renewable energy to strengthen regional areas, said communities were calling for more clarity about the approval of projects and said call-ins could cloud that process. "Once a planning approval is given, then let's go ahead with it. If it's not, then we can move on to something else," he said. Andrew Bray says both regional communities and investors simply want clarity when it comes to the approval process for wide scale energy projects. ( Picture: ABC Southern Qld/Aisling Brennan ) Mr Littleproud said while he was "not against renewables", the Tarong West Wind Farm should be scrapped, citing concern from communities about the workers camp and the project. While calling for a duplication of Cogan Creek Power Station to support the Western Downs Digital Park, he said renewable projects should not "litter the landscape" and take "away our food security". He suggested a range of options should be on the table to manage the energy demands of hyper-scale data centres. "I think we've got the opportunity to get this right with baseload power, gas, coal, nuclear — if we're brave enough, and I think we should be brave enough — and put all the options on the table because this is the new frontier," Mr Littleproud said. "This is the next industrial revolution. We can't put our heads in the sand and go, 'This is all going to go away.' It's not." Two wind turbines projects on the Western Downs have been called-in by the state government to assess whether they go ahead or not. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) Queensland Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki said the state government was committed to renewable energy projects, adding that Queensland had more large-scale wind and solar projects committed to than anywhere else in Australia. Mr Janetzki said the state's energy plan was "all about the getting the balance right" between coal, gas and private-sector-investment renewable projects, which included the Tarong West Wind Farm. "We've got applications processes and we've given the community a chance to have their say, and that's an important process," he said. "We're open for business and that means renewable in the private sector and that's an important thing to make clear. "That shows we have a balanced approach and that'll be our approach for any future data centre proposals.

events.title: Iran’s economy faces another blockade: Red tape and gridlock are clogging up land routes that bypass the U.S. Navy’s Hormuz stranglehold
events.summary: The U.S. naval blockade on Iran is already crushing its economy, and efforts to divert shipments over land are not providing much relief. Before the war, more than 80% of Iran’s trade tonnage transited by sea via southern ports, but that’s been closed off. U.S. Central Command said Sunday, it has redirected 109 commercial vessels to ensure compliance with the blockade. As a result, convoys of trucks have flooded land routes along Iran’s borders with Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iraq, and Turkmenistan. Iran’s trade with Turkey, for example, jumped 19% to $3.2 billion during the first half of the year. But bureaucratic hurdles, such as long customs checks, and infrastructure that wasn’t designed to handle so much volume have produced massive traffic jams. At one crossing with Turkey, 3,700 trucks were stranded on the Iranian side. Lines of trucks stretch for miles, and drivers sometimes wait more than three weeks to finally bring their cargoes across a border. During that time, perishable foods go bad, and delays for other essentials add to costs, with inflation now at 90%. A Turkish truck driver hauling used cars into Iran told the Financial Times that wait times at the border on the return trip can reach 24 days. And an Iranian trucker said he spent 23 days waiting at a crossing along the Afghanistan border in mid-June. At the border with Turkmenistan, lack of warehouses and proper registration processes have limited the ability to transport more goods by rail, according to the Wall Street Journal . While bilateral trade with Iran’s neighbors is up, overall trade is still down. In the five months ending Aug. 22, Iranian customs show that non-oil exports fell 28% from a year ago to $15 billion, and imports dropped by 26% to $17 billion. The collapse in trade has hit fuel supplies, much of which must be imported as Iran lacks sufficient capacity to refine the oil it produces. That’s led to gasoline shortages, forcing Tehran to curb demand with price hikes. Given the all the problems associated with using land routes, Iranian industry admitted the Strait of Hormuz has to reopen. “Under these circumstances, there is little alternative but to find a way to restore and maintain the southern trade corridors” through the Gulf, a member of Iran’s Chamber of Commerce told the FT . President Donald Trump is counting on economic warfare to bring an end to the conflict, and even Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has expressed anxiety about the economy . But experts have cautioned that Iran’s repressive regime is unlikely to be swayed by the suffering of ordinary citizens and is prepared to wait out economic hardship longer than the U.S. public can endure high gas prices. An F/A-18 Super Hornet, attached to Strike Fighter Squadron (VFA) 102, lands aboard Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George Washington (CVN 73), Sept. 13, 2026. U.S. Navy Still, the additional cost of relying on land routes is also staggering. Majidreza Hariri, the head of the Iran-China Joint Chamber of Commerce, said last month that transporting a single container between Iran and China via ships costs about $3,000, according to Hariri. But bypassing the blockade by transporting it over land would boost the cost to $12,000. Given that 2 million containers pass through Iran’s southern ports annually, he estimated that heavier trade burdens will translate to about $18 billion in additional transportation costs alone every year. Relying on land routes to get around the blockade could provide enough necessities to allow for short-term survival, but the economy will eventually “grind to a halt,” Hariri predicted. By contrast, the other oil-producing countries in the Persian Gulf are getting more oil through the Strait of Hormuz, despite Iran’s efforts to scare away shipping with drone and missile attacks. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said Saturday the U.S. military has supported the transit of 1 billion barrels of oil through the strait over the past two months, while assisting over 2,000 commercial ships.  With the strait’s primary transit lanes now cleared of mines, the volume of crude oil, cargo, and liquid natural gas over the past two weeks was the highest in six months, or right after the Iran war began. “And Iran has exported zero barrels thanks to our ironclad blockade,” Cooper said. events.title: Qatar PM describes fallout of US-Israel war on Iran as ‘earthquake’
events.summary: Qatar shifts investment focus to $38bn domestic infrastructure plan Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani has called on states to respect sovereignty as a condition for security in the Middle East, warning against “cycles of escalation” after “an earthquake” caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran. The region needs a “framework in which sovereignty is respected” and no state can pose a “threat to another”, Sheikh Mohammed said on Sunday at the opening of the Qatar Economic Forum’s UN General Assembly-adjacent event in New York City. list 1 of 3 Israel started an anti-Qatar campaign, then scrapped it list 2 of 3 Michelle Bachelet exits UN chief race after low poll support list 3 of 3 Iran says conditions to re-engage in talks, end war sent to US via Qatar Sheikh Mohammed – who is also Qatar’s foreign minister – described the economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran as “an earthquake” with “its shock waves” reaching far beyond the borders of the Middle East, “challenging assumptions about security and stability”. “During the crisis, almost every conversation began with security and de-escalation, then turn[ed] to energy supplies, shipping routes, and with our investments, plans will continue. These were different expressions of the same question. When so much is being disrupted, what can still be relied upon?” He said that Qatar has weathered the test to the “foundations” of the country’s economy and security, but acknowledged that the ongoing conflict in the region is having an impact. “Permanent security cannot be built through arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity,” Sheikh Mohammed said. “We must address the sources of tensions and build confidence.” Reporting from New York, Al Jazeera’s Kristen Saloomey said that message “no doubt will be repeated” when Gulf leaders meet US President Donald Trump on Tuesday during the UN General Assembly. The PM also outlined a domestic shift in Qatar’s investment strategy by pledging more than $38bn in spending on Qatari infrastructure over the next five years. “That’s meant to attract private investors and send a message of Qatar’s resilience,” Saloomey said, while the PM is nonetheless acknowledging that the ongoing conflict is “having an impact on the region”. The UNGA starts on Monday and ends on Friday. The situation in the Middle East and its global ramifications are expected to be high on the agenda during speeches and diplomacy. Also on Sunday, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed Al-Ansari, told US media in New York that the mediation efforts by his government are ongoing to restart talks between Tehran and Washington to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

events.title: Shein, Temu shoppers do not feel responsible for environmental concerns, study finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ultra-fast fashion buyers feel a lack of personal responsibility despite environmental concerns A new study of ultra-fast fashion buyers found price was one of the biggest shopping motivators. ( AP: Richard Drew ) Shoppers of ultra-fast fashion companies, such as Shein and Temu, say despite being aware of environmental and ethical concerns, other factors such as price, convenience and not feeling personally responsible keep them coming back. A new study published in the Journal of Global Fashion Marketing this week found millennials, who frequently expressed concern about ethical and sustainability issues, often did not translate this concern into purchasing behaviour. The study surveyed 20 Australian millennials who shopped on ultra-fast fashion sites about what informed their purchasing behaviours. It found affordability, convenience, promotions, social media trends, novelty, variety and social validation were the biggest purchase drivers. For some, affordability meant they were likely to purchase styles they may not usually try and make riskier choices. You can get five things for the price of one at other places. I can redo my wardrobe every season without hurting my bank account. It's perfect when I need something quick and cheap for an event. The study also found the purchases were usually not spontaneous, with many shoppers saying they saved carts and waited for a sale before purchasing. When I see a 70 per cent off notification, it's almost impossible not to look. It feels like I'm losing money if I don't buy it. Sales get me every time. I've bought outfits I didn't even wear just because they were on sale. I add things to my cart and wait for payday or a discount notification. Study co-author Carol Tan, who is an associate professor at the School of Fashion and Textiles at RMIT University, said this behaviour was known as "strategic spontaneity". "You think it's impulsive, but it's actually planned," she said. "So what people do is they save the items, they have a wish list, and then they monitor their sales and wait for payday. "It could be sitting in their cart for a week or a month, and then a spur-of-the-moment decision is when they actually make the purchase and it happens in minutes." Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au The fast and ultra-fast fashion gap While fast fashion has been around for some time, platforms such as Shein and Temu differ in their production and distribution methods. Traditional fast-fashion brands release a new collection every two to four weeks that can range from hundreds to thousands of styles and sell primarily through physical stores. Ultra-fast fashion stores produce 2,000 to 10,000 new styles daily and use digital-only, mobile app-dominant sales models. Dr Tan said the rise of ultra-fast fashion has pushed some fast-fashion brands to change their strategy. "They are trying to not compete with the Sheins of the world and they are trying to go a bit more upmarket. So they sell better-quality stuff and they have like $400 jackets," she said. Outside of the growing price gap between fast fashion and ultra-fashion fashion, Dr Tan said these sites often sold items you could not buy in brick-and-mortar stores. Despite participants expressing concerns about the environmental and ethical impacts of ultra-fast fashion brands, many still continued to purchase on Shein or Temu. According to the latest figures from the Australia Institute, on average Australians purchase 56 items of clothing a year. It also reports more than 200,000 tonnes of clothing end up in Australian landfills each year. The study found participants were more influenced by social and economic drivers than long-term ethical concerns. I know it's bad for the planet, but when I'm on a budget and need an outfit for Saturday, I just block that out. I try to buy sustainable brands, but they are so expensive. Shein is just there and it's easy. If the big brands are allowed to sell it, then it can't be all my fault for buying it. I feel bad sometimes, but one small top isn't going to destroy the ocean. The study also found buyers would draw on explanations such as reduced feelings of personal responsibility, affordability constraints, limited access to sustainable alternatives and the belief that the individual purchases had little impact. In some countries, different taxes have been introduced to deter buyers from ultra-fast fashion brands. France has banned advertising from ultra-fast fashion businesses and introduced a fee that will rise to €10 ($16) per item by 2030. New Zealand has a levy of NZ$2.21 ($1.80) per package.

events.title: Charity provides school lunches for kids as food insecurity rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts National school lunch program launched in Moe aims to tackle food insecurity Victoria and Brandon are big fans of the Spoonfull program. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) A new universal school meals program launched in Moe offers healthy lunches to primary school children. The program aims to tackle food insecurity as well as improving student wellbeing and learning outcomes. The charity Eat Up hopes to roll out the program across Australia to schools in need. It is lunchtime at Elizabeth Street Primary School at Moe in Victoria's east. On today's menu, a chicken pasta bake is the hot option, and tuna and salad rolls are on offer for others. The children queuing up are told that the more they can stack on their plates, the better. "I love the food, it's amazing," student Victoria says. "My favourite has been the lasagne and butter chicken, and I really like the wraps they make. "They give options to us that if we don't like a food, then we can just try it and I just love how they do that." A team of volunteers helps to prepare the students' lunches. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The lunches are part of a program that aims to tackle child hunger and improve student wellbeing across the country. The charity Eat Up has launched its pilot program Spoonfull at the school, a universal meal program that provides every student at participating schools with a healthy lunch, every day. Ian Frost and Carol O'Reilly say they have seen a huge improvement since the program was introduced. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) The program was officially launched at Elizabeth Street Primary School in its purpose-built Hearts and Hands Learning Kitchen, after some strong lobbying by the school's wellbeing officer Carol O'Reilly. "I could see a need. I've been at this school for 17 years and I noticed running [the school's] breakfast club that kids are coming in without sandwiches," Ms O'Reilly said. "Now I know they're going out for recess with a full belly." She said learning outcomes and student welfare had improved greatly since the introduction of the program. "The kids are smiling. You can see them outside, they're playing and they're just dying to know what's for lunch." Students are offered a variety of healthy foods, including a hot lunch. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) School principal Ian Frost said the school lunch program had a positive impact on what students eat and had led to improved wellbeing and academic performance. Eat Up has been running for 15 years, delivering more than 6 million free on-demand school lunches to children experiencing food insecurity. Charity founder Lyndon Galea said the Spoonfull program built upon that business model to offer something more sustainable for schools to support students long-term. "This is different to our core model, [where] we have on-demand lunches, in terms of the cheese sandwiches, yoghurts and recess snacks," Mr Galea said. "We've learnt of certain schools where there's perhaps a higher number of kids arriving without food from home or where the socio-economic need bites even harder," he said. Lyndon Galea founded Eat Up 15 years ago. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) At Elizabeth Street Primary School, Spoonfull helped fund upgrades to the school kitchen to have commercial fridges and ovens, with hopes of also installing a dishwasher. Single-parent households and low-income families were at the highest risk. As the cost of living continues to affect families, so too has the growth in food insecurity. "Families who are already in a difficult spot are needing help more often and then a lot of families who have historically been just above that level of need and needing support are accessing food support for the very first time," Mr Galea said. Through support from Spoonfull, the school was able to make key upgrades to its kitchen. ( ABC News: Danielle Pope ) Eat Up hopes to have enough support to roll out similar pilots in two additional schools. "I think it would be phenomenal for Australia and something our country can really take a big step forward [in]," Mr Galea said. Elizabeth Street Primary School student Victoria agreed and said she thought all schools could benefit from the program.

events.title: Trump to meet with Zelensky as Russia-Ukraine attacks intensify
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after a phone call with President Trump on Sunday that the two will meet this week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Why it matters: The meeting comes as the White House works to broker an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to take reciprocal steps to deescalate and resume negotiations — and as fighting between the two sides has intensified in recent days. Zelensky's chief negotiator and the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, Rustem Umerov, told Axios he's been working with White House envoys in recent days to organize the meeting, which is expected to happen Tuesday. Driving the news: The meeting will take place several days after Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill and approved the biggest arms deal between the U.S. and Ukraine since assuming office — two steps Ukraine has been pushing for months. What he's saying: "An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelensky wrote on X. Zelensky said Ukraine is ready "to take really serious steps" to reach a deescalation deal with Russia. Behind the scenes: A source familiar with the call said Trump repeatedly asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The strikes are driving up global diesel prices. "The word diesel came up many times during the call," the source said. The intrigue: Earlier this week the Kyiv Independent reported that the Ukrainian government was "growing increasingly frustrated" with White House envoy Steve Witkoff. The story came out several days after Witkoff and Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time since the war began. Umerov told Axios the story was false. "I believe that the work of American negotiators should be assessed by people who are directly involved in the negotiation process and work closely with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," he said. He added that he's been working with Witkoff and Kushner on a daily basis over the last year. "Our main focus is on finding solutions for ending the war and gaining security guarantees and prosperity to Ukrainian people," he added. Umerov said the negotiations are under close public and media scrutiny and therefore "it comes with criticism." "Nevertheless, we need to stay focused. Steve has done a great job with us. We do not waste time and stay focused on finding solutions," he said. State of play: Umerov said significant progress has been made in the talks. "In particular, the number of stumbling blocks reduced from dozens to essentially one or two key issues that remain subject to negotiations," he said. "The trend is positive. The U.S. is super focused on the issue of stopping the war in Ukraine. The U.S. understands the situation on the battlefield, and signals to everyone that this terrible war should end," Umerov said. Yes, but: Hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have escalated in recent days, with both sides conducting more long-range attacks. On Sunday, Ukraine launched a missile attack on Moscow and hit an oil refinery. Russia has been launching missiles at Kyiv and other major cities almost every day in recent weeks. While Russia has signaled willingness to consider steps to deescalate ahead of winter — and a resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine — there has been little progress towards an actual deal.

events.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang says AI CEOs have 'ulterior reasons' for warning about doomsday
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI leaders are being disingenuous in their calls for more regulation. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says AI leaders are being disingenuous when calling for a slowdown. Huang said current regulations are enough to ensure the tech remains safe and profitable. Huang's comments echo those of President Donald Trump. Don't let the black leather jacket fool you, Jensen Huang isn't a doomer. Nvidia's CEO said as much in an interview with CBS News aired on Sunday. He accused the leaders of the frontier AI labs of being disingenuous in their warnings that, without more AI oversight, the products they are building could harm humanity in myriad forms. "Go and read between the lines," Huang said, referring to AI leaders calling for government regulation of the industry . "They're actually not asking for more laws. They're asking to be relieved of the laws we do have." "They must be doing it for ulterior reasons," he added. Huang said he didn't know exactly what those ulterior reasons are, but that scaring people about the tech is "irresponsible" and "unnecessary." Huang's comments on Sunday echo those of President Donald Trump, who said on Saturday that new regulations aren't needed to ensure the tech remains safe. "We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," the president said on Truth Social, his social media platform. Michael Kratsios , the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, has also rejected the idea that tech companies need government intervention to ensure the safety of their AI models. In a Fox News interview on Sunday, he said the AI labs could just go ahead and "just stop" if they think their products are dangerous. Last week, a chorus of leading AI CEOs said AI development should be slowed down until adequate risk-prevention measures could be put in place. In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-pronged plan that would, in his view, strengthen safeguards to ensure AI remains under the control of human engineers. One of those prongs included calls for the US government, "for antitrust reasons," to regulate frontier AI labs. Amodei's essay was signal-boosted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Huang has emerged as a prominent anti-regulation voice, together with Trump and David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech. In the CBS interview, Huang reiterated previous concerns that a slowdown among US labs would cede ground to China in the global AI race, and that AI labs don't need government help to implement a slowdown. "We don't need more regulations," Huang said. "We need to apply the current regulations we have." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Australians love these cars. Experts have 'real security concerns'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts We got a cybersecurity expert to hack this BYD. It was too easy On a narrow country road outside Canberra, I'm driving a BYD Shark 6, the hybrid ute loved by tradies and even a cabinet minister. But while I'm at the wheel, I'm not the only one in control; a hacker has access to the car. As the 2.6 tonne ute rounds a bend, he gets to work. With the stroke of a key, he kills the headlights, plunging me into darkness. The attack is not a total surprise. The Shark has spent the past two weeks with Dan Hreszczuk, a cybersecurity expert who specialises in cars. His task was to hack the vehicle and find out what could be seen and done remotely by the Shark's Chinese manufacturer. "It was easier than we were expecting," Hreszczuk says. Modern connected cars, particularly EVs and hybrids, are increasingly run by software, giving manufacturers the power to change, update and control vehicles, like never before. In the case of BYD and others, that software is controlled from China. With fuel prices on the rise, EVs and plug-in hybrids like the Shark have gone mainstream this year, making up almost a third of new cars sales to date. More than half of these are from Chinese brands. EVs, with all their sensors, cameras and microphones, hoover up and spit out vast amounts of data. Experts say that data poses a greater risk in the hands of Chinese EV makers because they can be compelled by the country's national security laws to co-operate with authorities. To put this potential access to the test, it made sense to pick a model from China's top EV brand, BYD. Hreszczuk, the co-founder of Fortify Labs in Canberra, was stunned by the BYD Shark's lack of cybersecurity. "The access we took advantage of didn't even have a password," he says. This lack of a password allowed Hreszczuk to access the car's digital arteries. From there it was a matter of unpicking the software programs which controlled different functions in the car. After two weeks, Hreszczuk was ready. Sitting by the side of the country road, he demonstrates what can be done with remote access to a vehicle. First, he locks the doors while I'm inside, blasts music over the speakers and plays images on the BYD's giant infotainment screen. Then, as I drive, he remotely switches the wipers on at top speed, sprays the windscreen with water and turns the lights on and off. The combination is unsettling and highly distracting. Adding to the distraction, Hreszczuk has the speaker telling me repeatedly: "For safety, use low beam." Fortunately, I was only travelling 30 kilometres per hour and the road was pretty straight. Then, Hreszczuk kills the lights altogether. Hreszczuk says he wasn't able to access more critical functions like brakes and cameras as these were well protected. But it doesn't take much imagination to understand how dangerous, even this kind of access could be in the hands of a malicious actor, with a vehicle travelling at high speed on a winding road. While sabotage is one worry, the concern most often cited is surveillance due to the array of cameras and microphones on an EV. Last year, the UK military banned Chinese EVs, even those made with Chinese components, from parking within 3 kilometres of some of its most sensitive locations. China itself has previously banned foreign EVs from military sites and political enclaves, aware of their surveillance potential. In Australia, there's no blanket ban on Chinese marques by Defence, but ASIO has warned ministers and public servants not to have sensitive conversations in their cars or connect work devices. But there's nothing to stop them owning a Chinese EV. Trade Minister Don Farrell has a BYD Shark 6, the same vehicle that Hreszczuk hacked. Farrell recently told a newspaper it's the "best ute I've ever owned". ASIO's surveillance fears appear well founded, based on what else Hreszczuk is able to do to with the Shark even at a low level of access. We devise a demonstration: I'll take the BYD for a drive around Canberra, and give my mother a call to talk her through some internet banking. As I drive past the war memorial and down Anzac Parade, Hreszczuk has already remotely accessed the vehicle and is tracking my progress. "How about we turn on the microphone?" he suggests to the crew back at his lab. At that point Hreszczuk can hear everything. When she picks up, I'm straight into the details of how I had set up her internet banking. "I'm going to use as a temporary password, my initials, the number of my house, and then my full date of birth. And then you can go in later and change it if you want," I tell her.

events.title: Is the AI industry really ready to slow down?
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt We’re seeing a big debate over AI safety and a potential slowdown, as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently published a plan to “pace the frontier,” while Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has publicly echoed President Donald Trump’s claims that the AI backlash is a hoax and regulation is unnecessary. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed whether executives like Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are serious about wanting to slow down. While I was surprised at how many industry leaders seemed to throw their support behind Amodei’s plan, Sean noted that the plan seemed short on details. And when Kristen asked whether a combination of existing regulation and the workings of the free market could provide enough safeguards on their own, Sean replied, “We have a federal government at the moment that certainly does not seem eager to enforce regulations broadly speaking, let alone specifically speaking here.” Plus, he argued, “There does not seem like there is a ton of consumer choice driving this market, in the sense of, okay, if one of these companies does something really bad, then they will see an impact in how many cancellations there are or whatever.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony Ha: Sean, what do you think? Are we actually going to”‘pace the frontier”? Sean O’Kane: That sounds, for some reason, like something from “Point Break.” It’s just a very California statement, like, “We’re gonna pace the frontier, bruh.” I don’t know. I said on this show last week , I didn’t think we were headed for a slowdown of any kind, in large part because I don’t think these companies are structured in a way where that works. So this was a pretty immediate flip of what I said a week ago, to hear this from Dario at Anthropic and Sam at OpenAI and even Elon Musk to a certain degree — and we can get into whether we believe that or not. I will say, I don’t think I was completely wrong, because even with these loose plans that Dario laid out in a blog post and and some of the other leaders have talked about, I feel like we’re still missing a lot of specifics here, not only on some of the claims about why these people think there are dangers and risks, but also specifics on what they mean by slowing down. Anthony, I know you read this stuff pretty closely last weekend as it was all popping off, so I’m curious if you’re maybe more generous than I am, as far as understanding what it is they’re trying to say here. Anthony: I mean, I also have questions. What really stood out to me is the fact that so many people in the industry seemed to coalesce around this fairly quickly. Even before Amodei published his blog post, I was seeing other people post some version of this [plan,] just in the days leading up to it. My understanding is, these suggestions that have come out of the AI safety community; these are things that have been percolating for a while. They’re not just things that [Amodei] thought up on his own. But it just seemed like a lot of people were kind of ready to embrace this and in some ways, [it’s] encouraging to see that there’s a consensus. But it also makes me a little skeptical that this would represent genuine, major steps towards a slowdown. Kirsten Korosec: First of all, consensus can be a good thing. Also, it can be the beginnings of forming a cartel. And so, let’s be clear [about] who we’re talking about here. We’re talking about frontier AI labs. and that’s specific and important. You did say a minute ago that the details aren’t really clear, but we do know that the general idea here is that independent third party evaluators would come in that would work inside [companies] like Anthropic or OpenAI and monitor AI safety practices and incidents. But there is a lot of vagueness around that. Then there’s another proposal to have major AI companies in democratic countries coordinate on safety standards and limits. And then this international coordination piece. So those are the general ideas around this. I’ll also add that there’s been very considerable pushback from very specific people. And surprisingly, some people I didn’t think would push back on this. The obvious one, I guess, would be Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, who had some pretty choice words. I don’t know what either of you think of […] some of his comments and the call he took from President Trump on-stage [at the All-In Summit] Sean: I think Jensen understands that, to a certain extent, he is seen as the adult in the room here. Which is interesting, because that’s a dynamic that I think has changed.

events.title: My 13-year-old refused to share his location with me. I was annoyed — until I realized he had a point.
events.summary: The author (not pictured) didn't think she was a helicopter mom until her son pushed back on tracking. Carol Yepes/Getty Images I let my 13-year-old spend time with friends without constant supervision. When I asked to track his location, he argued that he'd earned my trust. I stopped routinely tracking him and now rely mostly on communication. I don't think of myself as an overprotective parent . I began letting my kids stay home alone for short stints when they were around 10. I let them wander our neighborhood alone starting when they were 11 or 12. I don't heavily monitor their social lives or phone usage, nor do I check their grades constantly or make them give me access to their Google Classroom to monitor their schoolwork. But I don't do things the same way that my generation's parents did things. I'm Generation X , and in my generation, there were no "playdates." Parents didn't track your grades, and they definitely didn't track your location. You'd be walking around the neighborhood alone at 6 or 7 years old, often for hours. Usually your parents had no idea where you were. The hope was that you'd come home sometime before dark. I didn't realize I was a helicopter parent When my youngest son turned 13, he started going out with friends on his own. Sometimes he'd take a friend's school bus home with them, and hang out for a few hours. Other times, he'd walk over to a friend's house, and then walk around town. I supported this — it reminded me of the freedom I experienced as a teenager and I know how important that was for my own development. My son is super responsible, and doesn't make social plans without letting me know. That's why I didn't think it would be such a big deal when I asked him to share his location with me on his phone. The author asked her teenage son to track his location. Courtesy of the author I didn't think of tracking as an invasion of my son's privacy. It just felt normal, the same way that I can see his grades as they come in on the school portal if I choose to. Or the way that I ask my son to text me about his social plans as they unfold, rather than just sending him out and expecting him to come back by nightfall. But my son was adamant about me not tracking his location . My first reaction was, "I'm giving you freedom to do whatever you want, so I should be able to see where you are!" But as he made his case to me — that he is responsible and will update me, but doesn't like the idea of me tracking his every movement — I totally saw his point. It's one thing to tell your parents what you're doing, and when you're coming home, but do parents really need to monitor every step a child takes? I understand the idea of knowing a child's location so that you might be able to find them if you don't end up hearing from them. But honestly, if something awful were to happen, there's no way to be sure they'd still have their phone on them, or that tracking them would be able to protect them in any significant way. Plus, I saw my son's point. I put my own teenage self in his position. If my parents had some way to track every move I made back in the day, I definitely would have felt resentful. It made me reflect on modern parenting After this happened, I realized that — without fully noticing it — I'd adopted so many overbearing aspects of modern parenting. I have a college student, and I see parents freaking out when they find out they can no longer monitor their kids' grades, and that kids (not parents) have to email the financial aid and school housing departments to take care of school business. The author says the experience made her reflect on modern parenting. Courtesy of the author Our kids are eventually going to be grown-ups, and if we don't begin to loosen our grips on them, I fear that they are going to go into adulthood completely ill-equipped to handle anything on their own. I know this world is dangerous, and knowing where your child is located may make you feel more confident as you let them venture out into the world. But you also have to consider your child's mental health and development and what it might mean for them to feel as though you are tracking every move they make. Kids need to feel like their lives are their own and that the world is a place they can explore without constant scrutiny. We came up with a compromise that worked for both of us Despite all this, I realized that certain aspects of modern parenthood and things like GPS tracking technology can be helpful. So my son and I came up with a compromise. For the most part, I don't ask him to share his location with me, but I expect him to keep me updated about his plans, and text me if he needs to be picked up or if any other issues emerge while he's out. But there are times when we end up using his phone's tracking feature, such as when he shares the location of where he needs to be picked up or when he's exploring an area that he's less familiar with. This balance has made sense for our family because it's based on open communication, deep listening, and giving my son as much freedom as possible so that he can mature into a strong, resilient, and independent young adult. events.title: Vocci’s ring adds a new form factor to meeting note-taking
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt There is no dearth of different forms of hardware for meeting note-taking , including pendants, pins, and credit-card-styled devices. That hasn’t stopped Vocci from releasing a new device for the same use case in a ring form factor, which is convenient but could create some privacy issues. The ring form factor is one of the easiest for anyone who wants to just press a button and have the device start recording. Pebble’s new Index 01 Ring, which I am testing right now, lets you hold the button and take a note or a reminder. Stream Ring, made by Sandbar, works similarly with a control pad on the top. Vocci’s ring takes a different path, with meeting note-taking as a central function. The ring has a button, which you can double-tap to start recording and double-tap again to stop. You can tap and hold the button to ask Vocci AI questions, but that only works when you have the app open. There is an indicator light and a haptic motor for recording feedback. The ring is lightweight at under 6 grams and uses titanium material on the inner and outer surfaces — likely a coating. The company claims that the Vocci ring can record notes for 8 hours on a single charge. The device comes with a chunky plastic case, which can charge the ring up to three times. The device captures meetings very well. I have had conversations spanning more than an hour in loud cafes, and the ring managed to convert most of the chat into accurate transcripts. However, this method of note-taking is not great if you want to take short notes. The software is the disappointing part of the Vocci ring. The app itself is a bit confusing. Whenever I took shorter notes, I saw AI-generated insights that were longer than the notes themselves. Each recording has Chat, which is the main transcript; Highlights, which are short snippets you can capture by pressing the button while recording a conversation; and Notes, which is a summary and insight of the whole conversation. In the app, there is a tab called Base where you can find transcripts, recordings, and anything you generate from them, and I found that redundant. I didn’t find a way to directly initiate a chat with AI for session transcripts. Voice-enabled rings are a great form factor for taking short notes or reminders. The app doesn’t have direct integration with reminder apps, which is a bummer. The feature rollout for its software is also slow. The company informed me that users can use Vocci’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect to other assistants, but the option to do that didn’t appear until a few weeks ago in the app. Other meeting notetakers are building their platforms to allow users to automate insights and workflow through AI, and at the moment, Vocci’s platform is not fully built out for that. There are some privacy concerns with this device because of its form factor. Vocci’s ring looks like a regular piece of jewellery until someone notices the button on it. The ring has a recording indicator, but it faces the user. It’s best practice to let someone know that you are recording a conversation, and it’s also required by law in some countries and regions. But with this kind of device, some micreants can easily choose not to disclose that information and record the conversation without anyone noticing. The company said it encourages people to disclose that they are recording, but that may not be enough. At $249, the ring is pricey compared to other notetakers like Plaud or Pocket , and that is due to the device’s lightweight form factor. The ring is for someone who doesn’t want to stick a gadget on the back of their phone, wear a wristband, or wear a pendant. On the hardware layer, a lot of these devices are combinations of some microphones, a battery, and a connection to the phone. We will likely see more variety in hardware meeting note-takers in the coming years, until users pick the specific formats that work for them. events.title: U.S. economy hits pivotal milestone: Spending on data centers and other information-processing hardware now exceeds housing investment
events.summary: Two decades after the housing boom reshaped, then tanked, the U.S. economy, the AI boom is similarly transforming the drivers of growth. Hyperscalers have poured so much money into building as much AI infrastructure as possible—and as quickly as possible—that investment from a handful of companies is expected to reach $1 trillion a year soon. Meanwhile, the housing market has been largely frozen since the COVID-era boom ended in 2022, when the Federal Reserve embarked on an aggressive rate-hiking campaign to rein in inflation. “We’re seeing a pivotal shift in the US economy: investment is shifting away from residential investment and towards computers,” Adam Shapiro, vice president at the San Francisco Fed, posted on LinkedIn recently. He pointed out that inflation-adjusted spending on information processing equipment, which includes data centers and computer hardware, now exceeds residential investment. According to data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, real private residential fixed investment was $748 billion in the second quarter, down 18% from an early 2021 peak. During that same span, spending on information processing equipment has soared 51% to $752 billion. “The AI investment boom is massive,” Shapiro added. He also noted that residential investment is more sensitive to borrowing costs, which have gone up alongside Treasury yields. The benchmark 30-year mortgage rate is nearly 7% as the 10-year bond yield has hit the highest level since 2007. By contrast, AI investment has been less sensitive to interest rates, even as hyperscalers have started issuing more debt to supplement drawdowns of their cash piles. Google parent Alphabet , for example, even reported negative cash flow earlier this year. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has also highlighted the eagerness with which AI companies are offering debt—no matter the cost of borrowing. “We are also seeing big corporate issuance. And a lot of that corporate issuance, I would say, is almost yield-agnostic, because the build-out for AI, the returns on that, the companies believe they’re going to be so high. They don’t really care what they’re paying,” he said recently. The onslaught of AI spending is expected to keep ramping up. S&P Global estimated last month that capital expenditures from Alphabet, Amazon , Microsoft , Meta , Oracle , and SpaceX will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025. The ratings firm added that the industry’s capex is growing faster than revenue, warning that the aggressive build-out could lead to overcapacity if future demand doesn’t pan out as expected. S&P sees 2028 as an inflection point, with revenue accelerating and capex flattening. Until then, however, operating cash flow from the six hyperscalers will collectively be negative in 2026 and 2027, it added. The breakneck speed of AI development has also generated immense political backlash that’s rippling through the midterm election season. A new NBC News poll found that 64% of registered voters said they’d be less likely to support a candidate who’s in favor of building a data center in their community. AI has also fed into the cost-of-living crisis as consumers grapple with higher electricity bills and prices for new smartphones and PCs. That’s added to angst with home prices remaining out of reach for many Americans. While increased housing supply would ease pressure on prices, availability has been limited. The supply of existing homes has been constrained by the “lock-in” effect of homeowners with low mortgage rates reluctant to give them up amid today’s high rates. And new construction has been weak as high rates weigh on demand while building costs grow. Housing starts fell 2.6% in August to an annualized pace of 1.275 million, led by a drop in multifamily projects. While single-family homes rose, permits fell, signaling muted activity in the future. Meanwhile, the National Association of Home Builders reported builder sentiment fell to its lowest level in a year. “The big picture remains that elevated and rising borrowing costs are holding developers back, supporting our view that the downward trend in housing starts has further to run,” Capital Economics said in a recent note. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: ScrollEd wants to turn textbooks into TikTok
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Society has spent a lot of time bemoaning our digitally addled minds and goldfish-like attention spans, pointing the finger of blame at doomscrolling as the reason we can’t just sit down and read a book or study for exams. But what if the solution isn’t to stop scrolling, but to rethink what we’re scrolling through? That’s the bet startup ScrollEd is making. The Palo Alto-based startup is pitching in the TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield 200 competition with the novel idea that if students won’t open a textbook, the textbook should open itself up to them — as a scroll. ScrollEd has built an app that allows the user to turn any text file — including dry PDFs or text books — into a feed that feels a lot like Instagram Reels or TikTok. As you scroll, the content shows up as AI-generated video, audio, text, or even interactive quizzes. Swiping up surfaces a new topic, while swiping sideways lets you go deeper into the one you’re on, with a quiz waiting for you at the end. “The younger generation is increasingly going short form, vertical feed only (especially the 18 year olds we’ve spoken to!), and this poses challenges for any kind of media that requires depth,” Utsav Gupta, ScrollEd’s co-founder, told TechCrunch in an email. “We want to meet them where they are…We just have to be deliberate about how we use it and choose not to maximize engagement on the platform.” “A short video can make you curious; following that curiosity can mean searching for another explanation or leaving the app,” Gupta continued. “We wanted going deeper to be as easy as moving to the next video.” Gupta bootstrapped ScrollEd this year alongside his co-founder and wife Rebecca Neff after the two both noticed feeling dissatisfied after doomscrolling before bed. Both are students — Gupta studies AI and human purpose at Stanford, and Neff studies computer science at the University of Pennsylvania. The startup is targeting educational institutions, corporate training programs, and individuals who “just want something better to scroll on,” according to Gupta. ScrollEd is following a freemium model, combining a free consumer feed with a paid ScrollEd Pro subscription and annual institutional licenses. Institutions pay to deliver educational material through the platform, in exchange for reports about engagement, lesson progress, and other data. In the coming months, ScrollEd intends to focus on its consumer launch, building its lesson library and source-checking workflow, and developing pilots for institutions. (The company will launch its consumer business at Disrupt, in fact. “We’re hoping to ‘disrupt’ social media and short form!” Gupta joked.) The startup is also building infrastructure that will one day allow educators to assess individual learners and adapt to their needs. “The ambition is a social network that’s better for you,” Gupta said. events.title: Trump's tech advisor has advice for AI companies worried they're building unsafe models: 'Just stop'
events.summary: Michael Kratsios, the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Tech leaders say the pace of AI development needs to slow down, and asked the government to step in. Trump's technology advisor, however, says companies don't need the government's permission to do so. The Trump administration has broadly supported expanding and accelerating AI infrastructure. There's a simple solution for AI companies that feel like their models are developing at a frightening speed: Hit the brakes. That's the advice Michael Kratsios , the director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, gave during an interview with Fox News Sunday. "It's very interesting that they talk about these issues, about how scared they are about potentially where the future is, and maybe they want to do a pause," Kratsios said. "Our position is, if you do believe that you're developing a technology that is unsafe or you don't want it out into the world, you can just stop it." He added, "You don't need someone to force you to do that." Kratsios pushed back against the notion that the US government needs to take explicit action for tech companies to take a breather. "They just need to slow down if they feel that they need to do so," Kratsios said. "I think the key thing to always remember is the US government has lots of tools in its toolkit to deal with these issues when they come up, and we've used them in the past." Ever since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in 2022, tech companies across the globe have become locked in a race to develop the most capable model. Doing so could mean dominating the market and securing steady profits, a huge win for whichever company comes out on top. OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are among the industry leaders. Many Americans have expressed concerns that those tech companies are moving too fast and, in doing so, putting public safety at risk. A Pew Research Center survey published in August said over half of the respondents were more concerned than excited about using AI more in their daily lives. Potential job loss was among the top concerns associated with AI. Critics have also pointed toward privacy and cybersecurity risks. In July, OpenAI agents breached its training parameters and hacked Hugging Face , another AI company. This month, a cybersecurity startup used Anthropic's Claude to hack OpenAI's codebase . On Friday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring. AI leaders themselves have long expressed concern about the products they are raising hundreds of billions of dollars to build. In a blog post earlier this month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the Hugging Face breach convinced him that the industry needs to take its foot off the pedal. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet," Amodei wrote. He suggested placing independent safety monitors inside the frontier AI labs and called for more robust government regulation. The blog post earned support from his industry peers, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI Elon Musk, and Google DeepMind founder Demis Hassabis. President Donald Trump , who has broadly supported expanding and accelerating AI development in the US, said on Saturday that his administration would not do anything that could "stifle" AI's progress. He also announced a new AI Force to coordinate responses when AI goes off the rails. The Trump administration supported the $500 billion Stargate Project , an initiative to expand AI infrastructure nationwide, and he signed an executive order to accelerate federal permitting for data center construction. He will host China's leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington, D.C., this week to discuss AI and trade. Kratsios told Fox News Sunday that it's critical to have conversations about AI with China. "The key thing that we want to talk to him about is avoiding shared risks, and that's something that I think we can have a fruitful conversation on," Kratsios said. events.title: Meta’s Muse TV ad is the latest sign that AI agents are going mainstream
events.summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, has been trumpeting Muse. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta released a TV ad for Muse, its personal AI agent, as it pushes AI agents into the mainstream. Muse can act on a user's behalf, sending emails, purchasing things online, and handling other tasks. Fears about AI agents going rogue haven't dissuaded hype about the new tech. The next shiny new AI thing has arrived: The personal AI agent . Once mostly the domain of Silicon Valley coders who used them to amp up their efficiency at work (and anxiety levels ), the AI agent is now being welcomed into the home. And with the release of Meta's new personal AI agent, Muse, the do-it-for-you tech is rocketing into the mainstream. "It feels like magic," investor Sheel Mohnot said on X in reference to Instinct, another trendy new personal AI agent . "Contrary to what some people have said, I don't think the appeal is limited to Silicon Valley types." These agents often live on common messaging apps. Users send messages, asking them to handle tasks like sending emails, purchasing things online, posting to social media, tracking prices, managing calendars, among many other things. In Meta's first television spot, released this weekend, for the Muse AI agent , a woman prepares for a dinner party — chopping lettuce, mixing drinks — while her AI agent autonomously sorts emails, arranges her schedule, and purchases back-to-school items online. "Muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you," Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, said on X on Saturday. muse is going NATIONWIDE to a television near you this is our first @muse ad ever, going live this weekend! we hope you like it while watching the big game(s)! big ups to @joshginsberg , denise, and the whole meta marketing team ❤️ pic.twitter.com/1zMUVgdKna — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) September 20, 2026 The appeal of autonomous agents is plain. While the famous chatbots from Anthropic and OpenAI that are changing the world are designed to answer questions, personal AI agents can act on a user's behalf, run entirely in the background, handle whole processes online, and ping you with progress updates. It likely won't be long until AI agents are all over the internet. If you really want to take full advantage of their potential, however, Muse and other AI agents require the keys to your kingdom, including your email, your credit card information, your bank accounts, and an array of passwords. "A mistake or manipulation could have real-world consequences, and that is terrifying," Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at internet security firm ESET, recently told Business Insider. Meta has taken pains to reassure users that its agent cares about keeping your information secure. In marketing materials, Meta calls Muse "an agent that respects privacy." So far, concerns about privacy haven't dissuaded consumers from jumping on the personal AI assistant bandwagon. One day after its launch, Muse shot to the top of the App Store. "Introducing Muse," a line of text on the Muse app reads. "AI that hustles for you." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that | Editorial
events.summary: The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that OpenAI claims its agents have solved the Navier-Stokes problem. But questions remain about how useful and independent its work really is O n 8 September, OpenAI claimed that its AI agents had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the most famous and difficult challenges in mathematics. Had a human solved it, they would have collected both prize money and plaudits from their fellows. The announcement instead ignited what some mathematicians have called an “ existential crisis ” in their field over the power of AI, and accusations that OpenAI misused human work . The maths behind Navier-Stokes is difficult to understand, but the critiques levelled by mathematicians will be familiar to artists, office workers, or anyone else concerned about AI. OpenAI’s results, like any arising from a large language model, depend on digesting work by human mathematicians. The OpenAI paper cites sources, but many believe the company didn’t give sufficient credit, especially to several mathematicians believed to be very close to a solution – bad form that erases human ingenuity and hogs all the glory. The mathematician Tristan Buckmaster also has concerns that work he was doing on Navier-Stokes using OpenAI’s Codex model was seen by the OpenAI team. OpenAI has denied directly accessing this material, but could not rule out that data from Buckmaster’s use of their products “helped improve our model”. This lack of attribution and compensation for the human labour that AI is built on has turned many against the companies that develop these systems. It has yet to be adequately addressed. This is a particular misstep in the case of mathematics. As many mathematicians have pointed out, AI firms are keen to use their models’ maths prowess as an advertisement . But they rely on mathematicians to check their – often sloppy and baffling – work, and to tell them if it is useful and how it might be applied. An AI-produced movie or vaccine would have a clear and obvious use, whatever its merits, but it will take time and human intellectual labour to tell whether OpenAI’s purported solution contains any novel mathematical tools or insights. This should be an opportunity for collaboration. It has instead become yet another source of alienation and resentment. Despite this, mathematicians are remarkably open to the use of AI, even as they commit their names to open letters denouncing tech firms. Most recognise that the technology is undeniably powerful and particularly good at maths. There has been a nuanced discussion of how maths might change and integrate AI, with humans guiding and interpreting its work. There has also been some soul-searching as to whether celebrating the person – or machine – that achieved a flashy final result in the form of a mathematical proof is the best way to value contributions. As Bill Thurston, the Fields Medal-winning mathematician, put it in 2010, well before the age of AI: “The product of mathematics is clarity and understanding. Not theorems, by themselves.” These are still uniquely human qualities. Some critics of AI are still stuck dismissing its outputs as uniformly useless “slop”. AI will not become good at everything. But more people may find themselves in the current position of mathematicians, confronted with the undeniable effectiveness of AI, while deeply concerned about how it is being used. This anxiety might not exist, the mathematician Nestor Guillen wrote recently, if we could separate the tech from the tech companies, and democratise its use. It is increasingly urgent that we find ways to do so.

events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: How do we know when an AV is safe enough?
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Back by popular demand: Save up to $300 on Disrupt Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! One of the stickier problems for autonomous vehicle developers, regulators, and the public is determining when self-driving technology is safe enough for the road. So far, that question has largely fallen to industry to answer — companies that are applying their autonomous vehicle technology to self-driving trucks, robotaxis, and maybe someday personally owned passenger vehicles. Today, there is no standardized test for judging how well an automated driving system performs in the real world. We require people to pass a driver’s test before getting a license, but there isn’t an equivalent test or system for autonomous vehicle technology. So how do we know whether an AV is a safe driver? The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration says it’s working on an answer. Federal motor vehicle safety standards (FMVSS) already govern the vehicle automakers sell today. But those FMVSS rules weren’t designed for vehicles like the Tesla Cybercab and Zoox robotaxi, which lack traditional, and federally required, equipment like pedals, steering wheels, and design features like side mirrors and rearview mirrors. The NHTSA is working on a federal automated vehicle framework that it says will put safety at the foundation without stifling innovation, or as Administrator Jonathan Morrison put it this week, force the agency to play “whack-a-mole” with policy decisions or try to predict how the technology will evolve. That’s a tricky recipe to get right. The agency took a notable step toward that goal this week by reaching an agreement with SAE to launch ASCEND, a government-industry initiative aimed at speeding up the development of data-driven AV performance standards. “Our top priority for this consortium is ADS competency, which will inform and accelerate a corresponding federal motor vehicle safety standard,” Morrison said at the AI Horizons Summit in Pittsburgh. “Ultimately, our ADS performance rulemaking will provide federal leadership in this space. By delivering an AV competency standard, we hope we’ll be able to address the burgeoning past patchwork of inconsistent state and local level requirements, and continue to encourage American innovation and promote the safe deployment and development of these vehicles on the road.” There is no timeline yet for when this consortium will produce ADS standards. But I bet the AV industry is already weighing in. Note: Want to hear Morrison’s complete comments? Check out this video of the AI Horizons Summit, and fast-forward to the 04:36:00 mark. We have a few things cookin’ but nothing quite ready to share. This is a reminder that you can send us tips! Email Kirsten Korosec at kirsten.korosec@techcrunch.com or my Signal at kkorosec.07, or email Sean O’Kane at sean.okane@techcrunch.com . Will Wall Street invest in a pure-play robotaxi company? We’re about to find out. Autonomous vehicle company May Mobility plans to go public through a merger with special purpose acquisition company ACP Holdings Acquisition Corp. in a deal that could raise more than $300 million at a valuation of $1.4 billion. There are other publicly traded companies working on autonomous vehicle technology: Aurora and Kodiak, which are both focused on self-driving trucks; Rivian; and Tesla. And while Waymo is not (yet) publicly traded, its parent company Alphabet is. It’s the same story for Amazon-owned Zoox. But May Mobility, which operates autonomous Toyota Siennas in three locations, says it will be the first public company in the U.S. focused entirely on autonomous ride-hailing vehicles. Senior reporter Sean O’Kane notes this will also be a test of May Mobility’s “asset-light” and “partnership-first” approach to autonomy. Other deals that got my attention … Autonomous vehicle company Beep has merged with Freebee , an on-demand public transportation firm based in Miami. Freebee co-founders Kris Kimball and Jason Spiegel will join as chief operating officer and president and chief growth officer, respectively.
